prompt.en: A free-space dipole sketch predicts a deep end null, but an installed wire near buildings still receives a station off its end. What should be checked before declaring the antenna faulty?

text.en: Whether ground and nearby structures have changed the ideal pattern.

feedback.en: The free-space picture is a starting model. Ground and surrounding objects can change installed patterns.

text.en: Whether every practical dipole must have the exact free-space pattern.

feedback.en: That assumes away the surroundings. The lesson warns that real ground and objects affect the pattern.

text.en: Whether a low SWR guarantees an exact end null.

feedback.en: Impedance match does not guarantee the free-space radiation pattern.

text.en: Whether a centre-fed dipole is actually isotropic whenever it is installed outdoors.

feedback.en: Outdoor installation does not make radiation equal in every direction.

explanation.en: Use the free-space pattern to reason, but do not treat it as a guarantee for a cluttered installation.

prompt.en: For a square full-wave loop, a learner calculates 306 / f and uses that value for every side. What is the right correction?

text.en: Use 300 / f on each side because loops use the free-space formula.

feedback.en: 300 / f is free-space wavelength. It does not fix the perimeter-versus-side mistake.

text.en: Keep each side as calculated, then shorten only the feedline.

feedback.en: Feedline length does not correct four times too much loop wire.

text.en: Halve each side because every antenna uses a half-wave total.

feedback.en: A full-wave loop is not a half-wave dipole. Four equal sides share the loop perimeter.

text.en: Treat 306 / f as the full perimeter and divide by four for each side.

feedback.en: The loop estimate gives total wire around the square, not one side.

explanation.en: Choose the antenna formula, then divide the total according to the geometry.

prompt.en: An end-fed wire setup produces transmit audio distortion that changes when station leads move. Which path deserves investigation?

text.en: Unwanted RF returning on station wiring because matching or counterpoise control is poor.

feedback.en: Lead-sensitive symptoms suggest RF in the operating area. Investigate return paths and common-mode control.

text.en: Only speech-processing compression, because all transmitted distortion begins in audio settings.

feedback.en: Audio settings can cause distortion, but lead-sensitive changes point to RF coupling that also needs investigation.

text.en: Only a broken dipole centre insulator, because every wire antenna is centre-fed.

feedback.en: An end-fed arrangement has different feed and return-path issues from a centre-fed dipole.

text.en: A guaranteed harmonic, because every lead-sensitive fault is an integer multiple.

feedback.en: Lead sensitivity does not establish a harmonic relationship. Measure before selecting that diagnosis.

explanation.en: Use the physical clue to trace RF coupling rather than assigning a transmitter-emission label without evidence.
